items.title: Spec-as-Contract Workflow — Discuss → Approve → Implement → Verify → User Accept

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: extension
labels.description: Issues related to the VS Code extension

labels.name: plan
labels.description: Issues involving plan mode

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

VSCode Extension

### What feature would you like to see?

# Feature Request: Spec-as-Contract Workflow — Discuss → Approve → Implement → Verify → User Accept

## Summary

I would like Codex to support a workflow where a collaboratively developed specification becomes the authoritative contract for implementation and completion.

This would go beyond a planning or discussion mode.

The goal is for the entire lifecycle of a substantial change to happen with full repository context:

**Discuss → Design → Specify → Approve Spec → Implement → Verify Against Spec → User Review → Complete**

The key idea is simple:

> Once the user approves the specification, the specification becomes the definition of done.

Codex should not consider the work complete merely because implementation has been attempted, files were changed, or tests pass. Completion should mean that every approved requirement has been implemented, independently verified, and accepted by the user.

---

## Motivation

My current workflow for substantial changes usually looks like this:

1. Discuss the feature outside Codex.
2. Work through architecture, edge cases, data behavior, compatibility concerns, and tests.
3. Turn that discussion into a large implementation prompt.
4. Give it to Codex.
5. Codex implements the feature and reports that the work is complete.
6. I ask Codex to audit its implementation against the original requirements.
7. The audit discovers something was only partially implemented.
8. Codex fixes it and reports completion again.
9. Repeat.

On a recent substantial feature, I had to ask Codex to audit the implementation roughly **30 times**.

Many of those audits discovered requirements that were partially implemented even though the previous pass had reported the work as complete.

This creates a gap between two things Codex is already very good at:

* reasoning about a codebase
* implementing changes in a codebase

The missing piece is a durable contract connecting the reasoning to the implementation and verification phases.

---

## Potential Duplicate Issues

There are related proposals for a [Plan/Spec mode](https://github.com/openai/codex/discussions/7355) and a [Talk/Discussion mode](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/21254), and I think these requests are all addressing parts of the same broader workflow gap.

This proposal is intended to extend those ideas rather than duplicate them.

A discussion or planning mode helps establish **what should be built before implementation begins**. This proposal adds the missing lifecycle after that point: once the user approves the specification, the specification becomes a binding contract that remains authoritative throughout implementation, testing, verification, and final review.

The primary distinction is that Codex should not be able to drift from the approved design, silently reinterpret requirements during implementation, or declare “work complete” while portions of the agreed specification remain incomplete.

In short:

> Discussion and planning establish the contract.
> This proposal makes Codex remain accountable to that contract until the user accepts the finished implementation.

---

## Proposed Workflow

### 1. Discussion Mode

Before editing code, Codex should be able to discuss the proposed feature while having full repository context.

During this phase it should be allowed to:

* inspect the repository
* inspect existing architecture
* inspect schemas and APIs
* inspect tests
* inspect related implementations
* inspect repository instructions such as `AGENTS.md`
* identify affected systems
* identify conflicts or ambiguities
* propose implementation approaches
* explore edge cases

But it should **not modify the repository yet**.

This is the phase where the user and Codex work through the idea together.

---

## 2. Living Specification

The discussion should produce a structured specification that evolves during the conversation.

The specification could include:

* functional requirements
* architecture requirements
* behavioral requirements
* affected APIs
* schemas and migrations
* compatibility requirements
* failure behavior
* edge cases
* security and tenancy constraints
* expected UI behavior
* test requirements
* non-goals
* known exceptions

Each requirement should receive a stable identifier, for example:

* `REQ-001`
* `EDGE-004`
* `ARCH-007`
* `TEST-012`

These identifiers should remain stable through implementation and review.

---

## 3. Repository Instructions Are Part of the Contract

All applicable repository instructions, especially `AGENTS.md`, should automatically become part of the implementation contract.

Codex should not silently violate repository instructions while satisfying the feature specification.

If the requested implementation conflicts with an applicable instruction, Codex should surface the conflict during specification work.

A deliberate exception should require explicit user approval.

For example:

> `ARCH-007` conflicts with repository rule `AGENTS.md / Persistence / Rule 3`.

The user could explicitly approve an exception for that work session.

That exception should then become part of the specification and verification record.

No silent deviations.

---

## 4. Explicit Spec Approval

Codex should not begin implementation until the user approves the specification.

The workflow might have states such as:

* Draft
* Review
* Approved
* Implementing
* Verifying
* User Review
* Complete

Once approved, the specification should become effectively immutable as the definition of done.

If implementation reveals that the specification must change, Codex should return to the specification phase and ask for approval of the change rather than silently redefining the requirements during implementation.

---

## 5. Requirement-to-Code Traceability

During implementation, Codex should attach concrete implementation evidence to each requirement.

For each requirement, the review should be able to show things such as:

* affected files
* classes
* functions
* methods
* modules
* schemas
* migrations
* relevant line ranges
* tests
* API endpoints
* UI components

For example:

### REQ-014 — Preserve historical references when a part becomes obsolete

Implementation:

* `PartLifecycleService.markObsolete()`
* `HistoricalMaintenanceRepository`
* `parts.schema.ts`

Tests:

* `part-lifecycle.test.ts`
* `historical-maintenance.test.ts`

Relevant code:

* `PartLifecycleService.ts:142–219`
* `HistoricalMaintenanceRepository.ts:88–133`

This would allow the final review to function almost like a pull request review organized by original design intent.

---

## 6. Tests Should Be Designed With the Specification

Tests should not be an afterthought added during implementation.

While designing the feature, Codex and the user should be able to define the expected test coverage alongside the requirements.

This should include, where applicable:

* unit tests
* integration tests
* contract tests
* migration tests
* regression tests
* failure-path tests
* edge-case tests
* backward-compatibility tests

A requirement should not be considered fully verified merely because some unrelated test suite is green.

The tests should demonstrate that the specific requirement is satisfied.

---

## 7. Completion Status Must Be Granular

Requirements should have explicit states such as:

* `NOT IMPLEMENTED`
* `PARTIAL`
* `IMPLEMENTED`
* `VERIFIED`

`PARTIAL` must never roll up into “complete.”

If even one required item remains partial, the feature is not complete.

This would avoid a common failure mode where the happy path exists and Codex considers the broader requirement finished.

---

## 8. Independent Verification Pass

After implementation, Codex should perform a fresh verification pass against the approved specification.

Importantly, this review should not trust its previous claims of completion.

The instruction should effectively be:

> Assume the implementation may be incomplete. Independently compare the current repository against every approved requirement and every applicable repository instruction.

For every requirement, Codex should provide concrete evidence.

Example:

### REQ-021 — VERIFIED

Implementation:
`InventorySyncService.reconcilePart()`

Tests:
`reconcilePart.test.ts:142–311`

Evidence:
Handles discrete inventory, bulk inventory, unavailable inventory, and the required physical-check state.

### REQ-022 — PARTIAL

Implementation exists for supplier closure propagation, but no test verifies behavior for historical supplier-part relationships.

Required action:
Add the missing behavior or verification before completion.

This would make auditing deterministic instead of conversational.

---

## 9. Final User Review

Once Codex believes every requirement is verified, the user should enter a final review phase.

This could present the specification similarly to a PR:

* requirement
* implementation evidence
* tests
* changed files
* exceptions
* verification result

The user could inspect the attached code locations, question misunderstandings, and request changes.

Codex would update the implementation and verification evidence as needed.

The workflow should continue until the user approves it.

---

## 10. Only the User Can Close the Contract

Codex should distinguish between:

> “Implementation pass finished”

and:

> “Work complete”

The latter should only occur when:

* every required specification item is verified
* every applicable repository instruction is satisfied
* every approved exception is documented
* required tests pass
* the verification pass finds no incomplete requirements
* the user approves the final review

Only then should Codex mark the work complete.

---

## Why This Is Different From Plan Mode

There are several proposals around discussion, talk, planning, and spec modes, and I think they are all circling the same useful area.

This proposal focuses specifically on the next problem:

**What happens after the plan is approved?**

A plan is useful before implementation.

A contract remains authoritative **through implementation, testing, auditing, and final acceptance**.

The important capability here is not merely:

> “Help me decide what to build before writing code.”

It is:

> “Remember exactly what we agreed to build, prove that the resulting repository satisfies it, and do not redefine ‘done’ along the way.”

---

## Why I Think This Matters

Codex is already capable of making very large changes.

As those changes become larger, correctness depends increasingly on maintaining intent across multiple phases of work.

Without a persistent specification contract, users currently have to manually maintain that intent by repeatedly:

* restating requirements
* auditing implementations
* finding partial work
* correcting misunderstandings
* re-running audits

A native spec-as-contract workflow would make Codex substantially more useful for serious engineering work.

It would also give users much more confidence in large autonomous changes because completion would become evidence-based rather than confidence-based.

---

## Short Version

I want to be able to sit down with Codex, with Codex having full knowledge of my repository, and say:

> “I have an idea.”

Then we work through the design, architecture, edge cases, and tests together.

We produce a specification.

I approve it.

Codex implements it.

Every requirement is traceable to code and tests.

Codex independently audits the repository against the approved spec.

I review the evidence.

We resolve misunderstandings.

And only when I approve the final result does Codex get to say:

> **Work complete.**


### Additional information

_No response_

items.title: CLI: no way to name a `codex exec` session (/rename is not handled in non-interactive mode)

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: exec
labels.description: Issues related to the `codex exec` subcommand

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: session
labels.description: Issues involving session (thread) management, resuming, forking, naming, archiving

items.body:
### What happened

`codex exec` creates a thread whose `name` is always NULL, and there is no
supported way to set it from outside the interactive app.

Tried on codex-cli 0.155.1 (Windows 11):

- `codex exec --help` — no `--name` / `--title` flag.
- `codex exec resume <id> "/rename Giraffe"` — the slash command is passed to the
  model as prompt text, not handled by the session. The model replied that it
  requested the title but could not verify it was applied. `threads.name` stayed NULL.
- Same result piping `/rename Giraffe` on stdin.
- `codex --help` has `archive` / `delete` / `unarchive` that accept a *session name*,
  but nothing that assigns one.

### Why it matters

Agent-to-agent setups drive Codex through `codex exec` from another tool. Those
sessions land in the history as unnamed rows, so there is no way to label a run
("nightly docs sweep", "PR 294 review") for a human to find later. Sessions created
this way are also not written to `session_index.jsonl`, so `codex resume` does not
list them.

The only route left is writing `threads.name` in `state_5.sqlite` by hand, which is
clearly not intended.

### Requested

Either of:

1. `codex exec --name "<text>"` (and the same on `codex exec resume` / `fork`), or
2. handle `/rename <text>` in non-interactive sessions the way the app does.

Related but not the same: #32143 (show the `/rename` title on the input bar) and
#24289 (auto-generate a thread name after the first prompt).

Two locally launched Python background processes and their controller stopped updating during a Windows-initiated Codex desktop AppX package update. [FINMIND_1538_SUPPORT_SANITIZED.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32434050/FINMIND_1538_SUPPORT_SANITIZED.zip)

items.title: App-server: coordinated per-thread quiesce and scheduled-work drain for lossless fork handoff

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

items.body:
### What feature would you like to see?

A host-supported handoff protocol for replacing one long-running Codex task with a fork without losing user turns or scheduled/event-driven deliveries.

The currently documented App Server exposes `thread/read`, `thread/fork`, `turn/start`, and `thread/archive`, but no per-thread admission fence that all clients honor, and no scheduler pause/drain with acknowledged transfer of queued or in-flight deliveries. A client-side read-idle → fork → reroute → archive sequence has a race.

### Reproduction / failure mode

With two independent app-server clients, client A reads an idle source and forks it. Before route cutover, client B submits and completes a turn on the source. The child lacks that completed turn. Archiving the source earlier rejects the turn but is not a safe substitute: downstream routes and scheduled deliveries have not yet been transferred and verified.

A SessionStart/UserPromptSubmit hook is not a sufficient universal fence: an already-loaded client may retain the prior hook set, hook failure/timeout is not a durable admission guarantee, and rejected input is not a replayable native queue.

### Minimal host contract requested

1. An atomic, per-thread, generation/epoch-bound admission barrier shared by all app-server and desktop clients. It must stop or durably queue new turns and report the exact last accepted/completed turn at the boundary. It should drain any in-flight turn before the fork snapshot or fail without moving the boundary.
2. A host scheduler pause/drain primitive for this source task that reports and durably accounts for queued and in-flight runs, plus an acknowledged transfer/resume to the child generation. A paused but already-dispatched run must not later write to the retired source.
3. A final compare-and-swap cutover/readback contract: fork at the fenced boundary; transfer event/watch delivery; prove child route and backlog; then retire/archive source. On failure, resume the source without dropping or duplicating a user turn or scheduled delivery.
4. A deterministic, no-model test surface for two-client turn races, in-flight scheduled jobs, crash/restart, repeated cutover, and rollback.

An equivalent API design is fine. The essential property is host-wide enforcement and durable evidence, not a particular method name. A cooperative plugin journal can make its own files recoverable, but cannot fence native clients or the host scheduler.

### Related request

#38289 asks for atomic idle-only admission for one proposed turn. This request is different: it needs a temporary source-wide boundary for **all** clients plus scheduled-run draining and cutover during a fork. It should compose with, not duplicate, that API.

### Environment

Reproduced with Codex CLI/App Server 0.142.5 on macOS, using independent clients and disposable tasks. No production task data or credentials are included here.

Bundled CLI: codex-cli 0.155.0-alpha.9.2.

ChatGPT Pro.

### What platform is your computer?

Mac mini with Apple M4 Pro, macOS 27.0 (26A428).

```text

```

### What issue are you seeing?

Recently, the loading spinner at the very bottom of the Codex sidebar has stopped going away. My projects and some recent chats are already visible, and I can still use the current chat, but the spinner keeps running below the last item. It is distracting because the app gives me no indication of what it is still waiting for.

I captured the sidebar on September 20, 2026 at 20:41:02 KST (11:41:02 UTC). It shows populated project and recent-chat sections, with a small circular spinner underneath. This is not a blank sidebar or a loading screen inside a conversation. I do not know which update introduced it.

The desktop logs from the same app run show two remote environments repeatedly failing with `Remote environment is offline`, along with `Thread catalog sync failed`. Reconnect delays grow to 20 seconds and stay there in the sampled interval. Meanwhile, `thread/list` requests return with `errorCode=null` in 1–3 ms. The local app-server also reaches the connected state at 11:40:57.988 UTC, and another remote environment reaches it at 11:41:11.200 UTC.

This makes the remote catalog/reconnect handling a possible cause, but I have not confirmed that it controls this spinner. The successful `thread/list` response lines do not identify their host, so they do not prove that every host's catalog finished loading.

1. Open the desktop app in Codex mode with saved remote environments. In this run, two are reported offline and another connects successfully.
2. Look at the bottom of the sidebar, below the recent chats. The project names and some chats are already loaded.
3. Leave the app open. The bottom spinner continues running while remote reconnect attempts and catalog sync failures repeat in the logs.

I have not tested whether bringing those two environments online or disconnecting them clears the spinner. I have not reset the app data or changed the connection settings during this investigation.

### What is the expected behavior?

Once the available chats have loaded, the sidebar should stop showing an indefinite spinner. If a remote computer is unavailable, I would expect an offline or retry indication for that connection without leaving the whole list looking unfinished.

### Additional information

This may be related to #39234, which describes an offline remote environment blocking the global thread/history index. items.title: macOS memory warning: Codex exceeds 14 GB during PowerPoint Computer Use, with UI timeouts

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: tool-calls
labels.description: Issues related to tool calling

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.915.31945 (build 9922), read from the installed desktop application's bundle metadata. Bundled Codex: `0.155.0-alpha.9.2`.

### What subscription do you have?

Not recorded in this diagnostic report.

### What platform is your computer?

- macOS 27.0 (26A428), Apple Silicon
- `uname -mprs`: `Darwin 27.0.0 arm64 arm`
- Physical memory: 18 GiB
- Microsoft PowerPoint: 16.106.3

### What issue are you seeing?

While Codex was automatically operating Microsoft PowerPoint through Computer Use, my Mac became severely sluggish. **macOS itself opened a system memory warning asking me to close applications. Codex was listed first, with more than 14 GB of memory usage.**

The primary symptom is the macOS memory warning and system-wide slowdown, not merely a high number noticed in Activity Monitor or a sum of process measurements. The warning and its displayed value were observed by me; a screenshot of that dialog is not attached.

The incident occurred on September 20, 2026, in the evening (Asia/Shanghai, UTC+8). The corresponding PowerPoint automation records show problems around **19:22–19:28 local time / 11:22–11:28 UTC**, while opening a presentation, inspecting windows, and exporting a PDF:

| Local time (approx.) | Recorded result |
| --- | --- |
| 19:22 | `Computer Use server error -10005: Timed out waiting for the application to read the clipboard` |
| 19:24 | `Computer Use server error -10005: noWindowsAvailable` |
| 19:25 | `Computer Use server error -10005: timeoutReached` |

Several tool calls in this sequence took approximately **44–59 seconds**. Some calls included multiple UI actions and a UI-state read, so these durations are for whole calls, not measurements of a single click. The exact second at which the macOS warning appeared was not captured.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

This is an observed incident, **not yet a deterministic minimal reproduction**:

1. Use the Codex desktop app on the Mac described above. At the later diagnostic snapshot, the app had been running for approximately 8 hours 40 minutes.
2. Have Codex use Computer Use to operate PowerPoint: open a presentation, inspect the UI, and export it as PDF.
3. During the interaction, observe severe system slowdown and Computer Use timeouts.
4. macOS displays its memory warning asking the user to close applications, with Codex listed first at more than 14 GB.

Other Codex tasks and test subprocesses were also running. Their contribution has not been isolated. This has not been reproduced with only one task, in a fresh app session, or with Computer Use disabled.

The affected task contains private presentation content, so its transcript is not included in this public report. Exact token-limit and context-window usage at the time were not captured.

### What is the expected behavior?

PowerPoint automation should complete or fail gracefully without pushing the whole system into a memory warning. Tool/helper processes and session resources should be bounded and reclaimed when no longer needed. UI operations should recover cleanly from application timeouts.

### Additional information

Read-only process and memory snapshots taken shortly afterward, around 19:31–19:33 local time, found:

- System swap in use: approximately **7.6 GiB**.
- Approximately **280 processes** in the desktop app's process tree in one snapshot.
- Sum of per-process macOS `top` MEM values: approximately **14.36 GiB**. This is an approximate diagnostic aggregate, may double-count shared memory, and is separate from the user-observed value in the macOS warning.
- In a nearby component snapshot: renderers totaled about **3.9 GiB**; other MCP processes about **3.1 GiB**; **108 processes using the bundled `cua_node` runtime** about **2.3 GiB**; Codex task/sandbox processes about **1.5 GiB**.
- The native `SkyComputerUseService` itself was only about **88 MiB**. Other memory belonged to the main app, helpers, and active test processes.

The `cua_node` grouping is based on executable paths. It does **not** establish that every process was actively performing Computer Use, was orphaned, or was leaking. Likewise, the current evidence does not establish whether PowerPoint automation caused the memory pressure, existing memory pressure caused the automation timeouts, or both contributed.

Please investigate process/resource lifecycle and memory growth around this workflow, including whether the PowerPoint UI interaction and the system memory warning share a cause.

Potentially related reports found before filing (same root cause is unconfirmed):

- #35994 — macOS memory warnings with many subprocesses during long-running Codex work.
- #40462 — sustained CUA runtime load after Computer Use.
- #39816 — accumulation of idle macOS Node REPL kernels and input lag.
- #44917 — unified-computer-use helper accumulation on Linux.

This report adds the current app version, a specific PowerPoint interaction, a user-observed macOS memory warning, and correlated Computer Use error records. Raw session logs, company content, local usernames, and private file paths are omitted.

### What issue are you seeing?

Turns are terminated with:

```
Selected model is at capacity. Please try a different model.
```

and the rollout logs classify every one of them as:

```json
{"type":"task_complete","last_agent_message":null,
 "error":{"message":"Selected model is at capacity. Please try a different model.",
          "codex_error_info":"server_overloaded"}}
```

**41 occurrences** between 2026-09-18 and 2026-09-20 (by local date: 09-18: 5, 09-19: 11, 09-20: 29).

**This is not a usage limit.** The `rate_limits` snapshot inside the same rollout files shows:

```json
{"limit_id":"codex",
 "primary":{"used_percent":4.0,"window_minutes":10080,"resets_at":1790440873},
 "secondary":null,
 "credits":{"has_credits":false,"unlimited":false,"balance":"0"},
 "plan_type":"pro",
 "rate_limit_reached_type":null}
```

**It is not the local environment.** `codex doctor` reports auth OK (ChatGPT mode), websocket handshake HTTP 101, inference endpoint reachable, no proxy, all local SQLite databases passing integrity checks.

Attribution over the 41 failures:

- model: `gpt-6-astra` 41/41 (only model in use)
- reasoning effort: medium 27, high 13, low 1 → effort is not a factor
- service tier in effect: `default` 36, `priority` (Fast) 3, unlabelled 4 → **enabling Fast does not avoid it**
- turn duration: median 19.8 s, P90 321.5 s, max 1022.9 s; 13 turns >60 s, 18 turns <10 s
- session concentration: 36 of the 41 failures came from a single long-lived session

items.title: Codex App: Collapse Tool-Call Cards by Default and Remove Blank Space After Collapsing

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

App

### What feature would you like to see?

I would like the Codex App to display tool-call cards in a compact, collapsed state by default, with an option to expand individual calls when details are needed.
The app should also provide a global setting that allows users to choose whether tool calls are expanded or collapsed by default.
Current Behavior
The Codex App expands tool-call cards, such as Desktop Commander file operations, by default. When a task involves many file reads or other tool operations, these cards accumulate and cause noticeable scrolling and rendering lag.
There is also a UI issue when collapsing some file-operation cards: the content becomes hidden, but the card still retains approximately the same vertical height as before. This leaves large blank areas in the conversation.
Steps to Reproduce
1. Run a task that requires the model to read multiple files.
2. Wait for several Desktop Commander tool-call cards to appear.
3. Collapse the “View file” content inside one of the cards.
4. Notice that the content is hidden, but the card still occupies a large blank area.
5. Repeat this across multiple tool calls and observe increased UI lag and excessive scrolling.
Expected Behavior
1. Tool-call cards should display only a one-line summary by default.
2. Users should be able to expand individual cards when they need to inspect the details.
3. The app should provide a global setting for choosing the default expanded or collapsed state.
4. Collapsing a card should immediately release the height occupied by its hidden content.
5. Consecutive tool calls of the same type should optionally be grouped to reduce UI clutter and rendering overhead.
Comparison
For comparison, Claude Code already provides a compact default presentation for tool activity, allowing users to expand the details only when needed. A similar option in the Codex App would significantly reduce UI clutter and improve performance in tool-heavy tasks.
Impact
Different models use different tool-calling strategies. Some models perform more segmented file reads, repeated checks, or retries, which can produce a large number of tool-call cards in a single task.
In these cases, the Codex App becomes increasingly slow and difficult to navigate. Default collapsing, correct height recalculation, and optional grouping would provide a substantial usability and performance improvement.
The attached screenshots show the interface before and after collapsing the tool-call content.

items.title: Enterprise control to enforce SSH-only remote execution in the Codex desktop app

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

Codex desktop app

### What feature would you like to see?

Add an administrator-enforced Enterprise policy that allows the Codex desktop app to connect to remote development environments over SSH while disabling agent execution on the user’s local computer.

Organizations with strict security requirements may require all software development and coding-agent execution to take place on company-managed virtual machines accessed through SSH. In these environments, local agent execution is prohibited.

Codex CLI can be used directly on the remote VM. The desktop app could provide a graphical interface to the same environment, but its ability to execute agent tasks locally can prevent organizations from approving its use.

The proposed policy should enforce the following behavior:

- **Remote execution only:** Agent tasks, shell commands, and agent file operations run exclusively on remote hosts connected through SSH.
- **Local execution disabled:** Users cannot start or resume local agent tasks, move remote tasks to local execution, or run tools and automations against the local computer.
- **No local fallback:** If the SSH connection is unavailable or interrupted, the app cannot fall back to local execution.
- **Administrator enforcement:** Users cannot override the restriction through app settings, project configuration, or per-task approvals.
- **Clear status:** The interface indicates that the organization enforces remote-only execution and identifies the active remote host.

The desktop interface and the components required to establish the SSH connection would still run locally. The restriction would apply to agent execution and agent access to local resources.

### Additional information

A user-selectable preference is insufficient for organizations that require an enforceable restriction on local agent execution. This control would enable adoption of the Codex desktop app in environments where development must remain on remote infrastructure.

items.title: [macOS Remote Control] Existing task missing from project; dragging does not repair placement, client restart restores projectId

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

ChatGPT/Codex desktop for macOS `26.915.31945`, build `9922`, read from the installed app bundle's Info.plist rather than the About dialog. Remote host app version was not collected.

### What subscription do you have?

Not collected for this report.

### What platform is your computer?

Client: macOS `27.0`, build `26A428`.
Remote host: another Mac, connected through Remote Control.

### What issue are you seeing?

An existing remote task appeared under its intended saved project on the host Mac, but outside that project on the client Mac. The client still appeared to recognize that the task belonged to that project. Dragging the task into the project did not restore its placement.

The task history remained readable. Another task in the same project displayed correctly.

Read-only diagnostics before restarting the client showed:
- `list_projects` returned the intended remote project and connected host.
- `list_threads` returned the affected task with `projectId: null`; the other task returned the intended project ID. Both reported the same remote working directory.
- The client's saved `sidebar-project-thread-orders` already contained both task IDs under the intended project.
- Neither task had an entry in the client's legacy `thread-project-assignments` map or `thread-workspace-root-hints` map, and neither was in `projectless-thread-ids`. These are observations, not a claim that the legacy maps are authoritative.
- Direct reading of the affected task succeeded. Reading it and repeating task enumeration did not repair the null project ID.
- No unavailable hosts or sources were reported.

There was also a path discrepancy: the saved remote project's path and a cached summary for the correctly grouped task used one folder name, while live task enumeration used another folder name. The relationship between those paths, and whether it contributed to the failure, were not established.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

The original trigger is unknown; these are the observed failure and recovery steps, not a deterministic clean-install reproduction:

1. Connect a Mac desktop client to another Mac through Remote Control.
2. Compare an existing task's placement under a saved project on the host and client.
3. In the affected state, the host shows the expected project placement while the client does not.
4. Drag the task into its intended project on the client. The task remains outside the project.
5. Check task enumeration: the affected task reports `projectId: null` even though its ID is already in that project's saved sidebar order.
6. Close and reopen the desktop app on the client.
7. The user confirms the sidebar is fixed. A subsequent `list_threads` check returns the intended project ID for the same task, with the same working directory and task update timestamp.

No task recreation, Git operation, or manual state/database edit was performed during troubleshooting.

### What is the expected behavior?

The client sidebar and task-list project association should converge with the remote host without requiring an application restart. Dragging an existing task into its intended project should reconcile inconsistent placement or display an actionable error.

### Additional information

The restart result suggests stale client-side state or a project-association projection problem; the root cause is unconfirmed. Please investigate consistency between remote task enumeration, sidebar membership/order, path-based project matching, and the drag handler's already-in-project behavior.

Related reports:
- #39764: a newly created local worktree task reports a null project ID until restart. This case involves an existing remote task and unsuccessful drag-based repair.
- #37021: task-list project identity disagrees with a direct local assignment on Windows. Here, the client-side legacy assignment entry was absent.
- #41214: multi-host sidebar consistency problems across restarts. In this case, restarting the client repaired the mismatch.

Observed 20 September 2026. Project names, task titles/IDs, host identifiers, absolute user paths, conversation contents, and raw logs are omitted.

items.body: ### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)? Powered by Codex & OWL Version 26.915.31945 ### What subscription do you have? Plus ### What platform is your computer? Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0 x64 ### What issue are you seeing? After a fresh reinstall of Codex Desktop, locally-executed automations (execution_environment = "local", defined under %USERPROFILE%\.codex\automations\\automation.toml) no longer appear in the "Scheduled"/"Geplant" panel. Only cloud-based automations are listed. This is not a display bug on top of a failed fetch — log analysis shows the client never even issues a request for local automations when the panel is opened. Local automations remain fully intact and continue executing on schedule in the background. ### What steps can reproduce the bug? 1. Have several local automations configured and running normally (confirmed via memory.md timestamps updating on schedule, and SQLite WAL file (codex-dev.db-wal) actively written to at expected run times). 2. Fully uninstall and reinstall Codex Desktop (MSIX package). 3. Sign in again with the same account. 4. Open the Codex sidebar → "Scheduled"/"Geplant". 5. Observe: only cloud-scheduled tasks are listed; local automations are completely absent (not paused, not archived — simply not queried). ### What is the expected behavior? After reinstalling and signing back in, local automations present on disk under .codex\automations\ should be fetched and displayed in "Scheduled"/"Geplant", exactly as before the reinstall. Actual: only cloud automations are shown; local automations are silently never queried by the client. ### Additional information Environment OS: Windows 11 Codex Desktop App (package OpenAI.Codex, MSIX): version 26.915.4065.0 (About dialog showed 26.915.31945 at time of report; package version differs due to MSIX numbering) Codex CLI: codex-cli 0.155.0 CODEX_HOME: default, %USERPROFILE%\.codex config.toml: sandbox_mode = "workspace-write", [windows] sandbox = "elevated" App reinstalled fresh (uninstall + reinstall) shortly before the issue appeared; fresh MSIX profile confirmed under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages\OpenAI.Codex_\LocalCache (created at reinstall timestamp) What was ruled out (to save maintainers time) Data layer intact: all automation.toml files present and valid (status = "ACTIVE", correct rrule, correct cwds). Automations still execute on schedule post-reinstall — verified via memory.md mtimes matching expected run times, and active writes to codex-dev.db-wal at those times. Codex CLI (codex in an interactive session) can see and use the same automations without issue. windowsSandbox/readiness IPC calls succeed with errorCode=null throughout the session — not a sandbox/elevation problem. Confirmed by running the app fully elevated ("Run as administrator") — no change. UI language switch (German ↔ "auto-detect" ↔ English) — tested repeatedly, no reliable effect on content (see note below). Mode switch (Codex ↔ ChatGPT) — restores the "Geplant" sidebar entry's visibility in some cases, but never its local-automation content (cloud tasks only). Full sign-out/sign-in, process kill (Stop-Process -Force on all Codex/ChatGPT processes), and system reboot — no change. Terminal shell setting (PowerShell vs. Command Prompt) — no effect. Checked config.toml trusted-projects / hooks — unrelated (separately confirmed and fixed a different, now-resolved issue: stale [hooks.state.*] trust hashes causing invalid transport in mcp_servers.codex_app, which is a distinct bug from this one). Key log evidence Captured response_routed IPC method names (method=...) from Desktop app logs (%LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages\OpenAI.Codex_\LocalCache\Local\Codex\Logs\...) across a full session that included multiple visits to the "Geplant" panel: account/login/start, account/logout, account/read, app/installed, app/read, chatgpt, client-status-changed, collaborationMode/list, config/read, configRequirements/read, experimentalFeature/list, externalAgentConfig/import/readHistories, fs/readDirectory, fs/readFile, get, getAuthStatus, hooks/list, ipc-connection-reset, mcpServerStatus/list, model/list, permissionProfile/list, plugin/installed, plugin/list, plugin/read, query-cache-invalidate, remoteControl/enable, remoteControl/status/read, skills/list, thread/attachment/list, thread/goal/get, thread/items/list, thread/list, thread/queue/list, thread/read, thread/realtime/listVoices, thread/resume, thread/start, thread/turns/list, thread-read-state-changed, thread-stream-following-changed, thread-stream-following-status-requested, turn/start, windowsSandbox/readiness No method related to automations, recurring tasks, schedules, or cron ever appears — not even one that fails or errors. This strongly suggests the client-side condition that decides whether to fetch local automations (likely tied to project/workspace state established at first run) evaluates incorrectly after a reinstall, so the fetch is never dispatched at all. Related (but distinct) existing issues #25393 — Automations sidebar badge/count disappears after update (cosmetic only, automations page itself remained usable). This report describes a more severe variant: the panel is usable but the local-automation content itself never loads. #12679 / #21882 — No relink flow for a project whose path changed. Not applicable here — the project path is unchanged and confirmed valid (Test-Path → True). items.title: [macOS] node_repl / Computer Use fails when CODEX_HOME is a symlink despite allow_symlinked_codex_home

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: sandbox
labels.description: Issues related to permissions or sandboxing

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Codex App 26.915.31945 / Codex CLI 0.155.0-alpha.9.2; also verified with a local debug build of main

### What subscription do you have?

Pro 20x

### What platform is your computer?

Darwin 24.6.0 arm64 arm

### What issue are you seeing?

When `CODEX_HOME` is a symlink, `node_repl` / Computer Use fails before the JS kernel starts even though `allow_symlinked_codex_home = true` is present in `$CODEX_HOME/config.toml`.

The failure is in Seatbelt preparation for `codex sandbox` launched through `CODEX_CLI_PATH`: writable roots under the symlinked `CODEX_HOME` are rejected before `sandbox_apply`.

Error (paths redacted):
`writable root <CODEX_HOME>/visualizations/<id> contains symlink component <CODEX_HOME>; symlinked writable roots are not supported.`

Root cause: `codex-rs/cli/src/debug_sandbox.rs` calls `create_seatbelt_command_args(...)`, and that wrapper in `codex-rs/sandboxing/src/seatbelt.rs` hardcodes `allowed_symlinked_codex_home = None`. Normal execution paths thread this opt-out through `SandboxManager::with_allowed_symlinked_codex_home`, but the debug-sandbox / sandbox-state path used by `node_repl` does not.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Use a symlinked `CODEX_HOME`, e.g. `CODEX_HOME=/tmp/codex-home-link -> /tmp/codex-home-real`.
2. Set `allow_symlinked_codex_home = true` in `$CODEX_HOME/config.toml`.
3. Start any `node_repl` / Computer Use session, or run `codex sandbox --sandbox-state-json` with a writable root under `$CODEX_HOME/visualizations/<id>`.

A/B check against the same config:
- Original `0.155.0-alpha.9.2`: fails with `symlinked writable roots are not supported` for both `--sandbox-state-json` and `-c permissions.node_repl={filesystem = ...}` forms.
- Patched build: passes writable-root validation and reaches `sandbox_apply` (or runs when not nested).

Minimal fix: add `create_seatbelt_command_args_with_symlinked_home(...)` and call it from debug sandbox with `codex_config::allowed_symlinked_codex_home(&config.config_layer_stack, &config.codex_home)`.

### What is the expected behavior?

With `allow_symlinked_codex_home = true`, writable roots beneath the opted-in symlinked `CODEX_HOME` should be accepted by every Seatbelt construction path, including `codex sandbox --sandbox-state-json` used by `node_repl` / Computer Use.

### Additional information

Patch/diff: https://github.com/openai/codex/commit/403b6b06f57b22b4d90ab4cb5648bd3975dc411b

Files: `codex-rs/cli/src/debug_sandbox.rs`, `codex-rs/sandboxing/src/seatbelt.rs`, plus macOS integration test `codex-rs/cli/tests/sandbox_symlinked_codex_home.rs`.

The commit link is only for the exact diff; the repro above uses placeholders and contains no local paths.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?
1. Have several local Codex tasks and at least one pinned Codex thread.
2. Select Codex in the top-left product selector and note the Pinned and Recents lists.
3. Switch to ChatGPT in the same selector.
4. Observe that the pinned Codex thread is still listed under Pinned, and the same Codex tasks remain at the top of Recents.

### What is the expected behavior?
ChatGPT view should list Chat and ChatGPT Work conversations only, and Codex view should list Codex tasks. Related report #42742 states that the Pinned section filters correctly, but on 26.915 the Pinned section also leaks a local Codex thread, so the leak is broader here. If a unified list is intentional, rows need a Chat / Work / Codex type indicator and the documentation should say so.

### Additional information
Impact: the same conversation opens under different rules depending on the view (Codex = AGENTS.md plus local harness with file and command access; ChatGPT = account custom instructions plus cloud environment), so it is not possible to tell which environment is active. Two screenshots from the same running session were captured; titles can be redacted.
Related: #42742, #36220, #35367, #33716

Side note: in the ChatGPT view, the "Codex and Work usage exhausted" banner still shows while the only active provider is a third-party one; not part of the main report.
### Local state evidence (text only, no logs)

On the affected machine (Windows 10 22H2, app 26.915.4065.0), the thread shown in both views is registered only on the Codex side.

Reading ~/.codex/.codex-global-state.json (read-only), the thread id appears in exactly these Codex-side containers:

- projectless-thread-ids[]        -> thread is a projectless Codex thread
- pinned-thread-ids[]             -> thread is pinned
- app-server-pinned-thread-order-v1[] -> pinned ordering
- client-thread-bindings-v1.*     -> local client/server thread binding
- app-server-projects-migration-by-host.*.pendingThreadAssignmentIds[] -> not yet assigned to any project

There is no ChatGPT-side or Work-side entry that references this thread id. The same result holds for the other local Codex tasks visible in the ChatGPT view's Recents list.

Implication: nothing in local state indicates that these threads belong to the ChatGPT product surface, yet they are listed in the ChatGPT view. The Codex view filters them correctly, so the filtering is asymmetric between the two views.

Difference from #42742: that report states the Pinned section filters correctly. On 26.915.4065.0 the Pinned section also shows the Codex thread in the ChatGPT view, so the leak is broader on this build.

Reproduction is text-only and deterministic: pin any local Codex thread, switch the product selector to ChatGPT, then compare the Pinned and Recents sections with the Codex view. No screenshots are required to observe the asymmetry.

### Codex App version

26.908.40834

Bundled Codex CLI: 0.154.0-alpha.6.2

### Subscription

Not provided.

### Platform

Darwin 24.6.0 arm64 arm

### What issue are you seeing?

The Codex App file viewer intermittently fails to paint the first lines of an ordinary source file. The missing lines still occupy their expected vertical layout space, but the area is blank. Rendering resumes at a later line; in the observed case, line 14 and everything below it were visible while lines 1 through 13 were absent.

The source file itself is intact. Reading it in the terminal shows every line, file reports ordinary ASCII text, and a byte dump shows normal LF line endings with no BOM or control bytes. This is therefore a viewer paint/rendering defect rather than missing or malformed source content.

The problem was also preceded by a file opening as an entirely blank surface when switching out of the review view. Reopening the file explicitly at line 1 did not repaint it; the app queued the open request instead.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Open a Git repository in Codex App.
2. Enter the review/file browsing surface.
3. Select a Go source file in the file tree.
4. Switch from the review surface to the regular file viewer, or move between newly created files and existing source files.
5. Observe that an initial contiguous range of source lines may be blank even though later line numbers and code render normally.
6. Verify the same file in a terminal with nl, sed, file, or od; the hidden lines are present and contain normal text.
7. Attempt to reopen the file at line 1. In the observed session this did not repaint the missing lines.

The issue occurred for more than one file-view transition in the same session. No application error was displayed.

### Expected behavior

The regular file viewer should render every source line present on disk. Switching between review and file views, including files newly created in the working tree, should not leave blank unpainted ranges or queue a file-open request indefinitely.

### Additional information

The blank region retained the exact vertical space of the omitted lines, suggesting that layout or virtualization completed while syntax-highlighted text painting did not. Closing/reopening the view was the only apparent workaround. No source modification is necessary to reproduce or recover the hidden content in another viewer.

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.description: Issues involving session (thread) management, resuming, forking, naming, archiving

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using?

Windows MSIX package version: **26.915.4065.0** (read from installed-package metadata, not the About dialog).
Bundled browser/computer-use plugin release: **26.915.31945**.

### What subscription do you have?

Signed in with ChatGPT. Exact subscription tier was not collected for this report.

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.19045.0, x64.
Google Chrome 153.0.8010.48; official Chrome extension 1.26.901.11451.

### What issue are you seeing?

An existing local task (Thread A) cannot access the bundled `cua_repl` tool after a desktop-app restart, while a newly created local `@Chrome` task (Thread B) in the **same running desktop application** can access it and successfully read/control the same signed-in local Chrome session.

This is more specific than a browser being closed or an extension failing to connect:

- Thread A exposes `node_repl`, `codex_apps`, and `codex_app`, but no callable `cua_repl/js`. Re-mentioning `@Chrome` and sharing a Chrome tab in A did not restore that tool.
- Thread B exposes all four services, including `cua_repl`. Its actual `cua.getState()` / `cua.getTab()` calls and subsequent browser UI operations succeed.
- Desktop logs correlate these differences with the individual thread IDs. The two tasks use the same local host and desktop-app process/session.

The native `@oai/sky` route in A can discover/activate Chrome, but attempting to read the Chrome window stops with:

> Computer Use has been stopped for this turn because it could not determine the current browser URL on Windows with enough confidence to enforce policy.

That route was stopped as instructed. This report does **not** request bypassing URL verification. The missing bundled browser tool and the native URL-verification failure are separate observations; their relationship has not been established.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed sequence on September 20, 2026; a deterministic minimal reproduction from a clean install is not yet established:

1. Have a long-running local task A. Logs from an earlier desktop-app process show `cua_repl` reaching `ready` for A.
2. Restart the desktop application and resume A.
3. Ask A to use Chrome, including an explicit `@Chrome` mention and a shared tab.
4. Observe that A lacks a callable `cua_repl` tool and its MCP startup events list only the other three services.
5. Create a fresh local task B with `@Chrome`, without changing/reinstalling Chrome or its extension between A and B.
6. B loads `cua_repl` and successfully operates Chrome, while A still lacks it.

### Sanitized diagnostic evidence

All times below are UTC on 2026-09-20. Thread identifiers are replaced with A/B. These are summaries of matching log events, not complete raw log lines.

| Time | Desktop process | Task | Observation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 08:02:08.988, 08:02:31.295, 08:10:03.452 | Earlier process | A | `server=cua_repl status=ready error=null failureReason=null` |
| 08:15:38.820–822 | After restart | A | Startup events for `codex_apps`, `node_repl`, `codex_app`; no matching `cua_repl` event |
| 08:56:43.206 | Same post-restart process | B | `server=cua_repl status=starting` |
| 08:56:43.378 | Same post-restart process | B | `server=cua_repl status=ready error=null failureReason=null` |
| 08:59:37.010 | Same post-restart process | A | Three services ready; `cua_repl` absent |
| 08:59:37.136–137 | Same post-restart process | B | All four services ready, including `cua_repl` |
| 09:00:08 and 09:03:09 | Same post-restart process | A | Same three-service pattern |

Earlier `ready` events establish that A had loaded the service, **not** that its earlier browser operations succeeded. B's successful operations are independently visible in its tool results.

Additional read-only checks:

- Official Chrome extension is installed and enabled.
- Native messaging host registration, extension origin, and executable target agree; native host has a valid OpenAI signature.
- No related blocking policy was found in the ordinary user/machine Chrome policy locations checked. This is not an exhaustive security-software audit.
- Browser, Chrome, Computer Use, and unified Computer Use plugins are enabled globally.
- A global `node_repl` entry with browser/sky trusted services is present and is available to both tasks. Its causal relevance is unknown; this is not a pristine default configuration.
- Runtime-path resolution events for A and B select the same currently installed Codex and CUA runtime executables. Different historical session-creation version metadata is **not** evidence that A is currently running an older binary.
- No project-level configuration override was found in the checked task directories.

### What is the expected behavior?

Resuming an existing task and explicitly invoking an enabled Chrome plugin should make its supported browser tools available, as in a new task. If a task's capability binding cannot be refreshed, the app should show an actionable explanation and a supported recovery path that preserves task history.

Please investigate why `cua_repl` is omitted for one resumed task but loaded for a new task in the same app session, and advise how to refresh/recover an affected task. The underlying cause (task binding, lifecycle, configuration, or another component) is not confirmed.

### Related reports

- #44518: session-specific `cua_repl` lifecycle failure on macOS; this report concerns an absent tool/startup event on Windows, not a callable tool returning `Transport closed`.
- #43880: Chrome native URL-verification failure on Windows, matching the fallback error class here.
- #45221: native Windows control unavailable despite `cua_repl` being ready; here the affected task lacks `cua_repl` entirely while another task's Chrome control works.

This public report excludes private URLs/page content, account identifiers, task IDs, usernames, absolute local paths, pipe addresses, screenshots, and complete raw logs.

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

ChatGPT/Codex desktop 26.915.31945 (build 9922), installed as `ChatGPT.app` with signed bundle identifier `com.openai.codex`.

### What subscription do you have?

Not supplied. The failure occurs while connecting a browser extension to its local macOS helper.

### What platform is your computer?

macOS 27.0 (build 26A428), Apple silicon (`arm64`). Built-in browser framework: 153.0.8010.48.

### What issue are you seeing?

The official Apple iCloud Passwords extension installs in the desktop app’s built-in browser, but clicking it shows:

> iCloud Passwords couldn't connect to a helper application on your Mac. Ensure that your system is using the latest version of macOS and that you are using a supported web browser.

The extension cannot reach its normal authentication/unlock flow, so iCloud Passwords cannot be used for autofill in the built-in browser.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Open the built-in browser in the ChatGPT/Codex desktop app on the macOS version above.
2. Install and enable Apple’s official iCloud Passwords extension, ID `pejdijmoenmkgeppbflobdenhhabjlaj`.
3. Click the extension’s toolbar button.
4. Observe the helper-connection error above.

### What is the expected behavior?

The extension should connect to Apple’s local helper and offer the normal Apple authentication/unlock flow, enabling password autofill in the built-in browser. If this integration is currently unsupported, the app should explain that limitation during extension setup.

### Additional information

**Observed locally:**

- Apple’s `PasswordManagerBrowserExtensionHelper` is present and executable at `/System/Cryptexes/App/System/Library/CoreServices/PasswordManagerBrowserExtensionHelper.app/Contents/MacOS/PasswordManagerBrowserExtensionHelper`.
- Existing Chrome native-messaging manifests point to that executable and allow the official extension ID.
- Adding an equivalent registration under `~/Library/Application Support/OpenAI/Codex/NativeMessagingHosts` did not resolve the reported error. That experimental registration was subsequently removed. The actual lookup path used by the embedded browser has not been instrumented.

**Suspected signing/entitlement compatibility problem:**

Static inspection of the installed Apple helper’s signed parent launch constraints shows that it accepts either a browser with `com.apple.developer.web-browser.public-key-credential`, or specific signing-identifier/team-identifier combinations. These include `com.openai.atlas.web` with OpenAI’s team identifier `2DC432GLL2`.

The installed desktop app is signed as `com.openai.codex`; its browser helper apps use `com.openai.codex.helper` or `com.openai.codex.helper.renderer`. Those identities are absent from the inspected allowlist, and the inspected app/helper entitlements do not include `com.apple.developer.web-browser.public-key-credential`.

This is a diagnosis from static signature inspection, **not a captured runtime launch rejection**. Narrowly filtered macOS security logs did not expose a rejection. Please confirm the runtime cause, the native-host lookup path, and whether the built-in browser needs additional Apple entitlement/allowlist support.

Relevant read-only diagnostic commands:

```sh
codesign -dvvvvvv /System/Cryptexes/App/System/Library/CoreServices/PasswordManagerBrowserExtensionHelper.app
codesign -dvv /Applications/ChatGPT.app
codesign -d --entitlements :- /Applications/ChatGPT.app
```

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.915.31945 (build 9922), read from the installed app bundle metadata.
Bundled CLI: `codex-cli 0.155.0-alpha.9.2`.

### What subscription do you have?

Not provided.

### What platform is your computer?

macOS 26.4, arm64.

### What issue are you seeing?

After closing and reopening the desktop app, an existing local Git project disappeared from the user's project list/sidebar, creating the impression that the project and its tasks had been lost. Another saved project remained available.

During investigation on 2026-09-20 at approximately 08:13 UTC, the app's supported tools exposed inconsistent state:

- `list_projects` returned only the other saved project; the missing project was absent.
- `list_threads` still returned existing tasks for the missing project with their original project ID and working directory. Its returned sidebar sections also still referenced that project ID.
- Read-only inspection confirmed that the project folder existed, the saved global-state project registration/order/selection still referenced it, and the core database retained the corresponding project and root path.
- A later `list_projects` call during the same investigation returned both projects again under their original IDs. The investigating agent had not edited app state, recreated the project, reopened its folder, or restarted the app before that successful read. The exact event that caused it to reappear is unknown.

No project-folder or task-record loss was observed. The confirmed issue is a temporary mismatch between the available-project listing and the retained project/task records. The underlying cause is unconfirmed.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed sequence, not yet a deterministic reproduction:

1. Have at least two saved local Git projects, with existing tasks under each.
2. Close the desktop app and reopen it.
3. Observe that one previously saved project is absent from the project list/sidebar, while another remains.
4. Query `list_projects` and `list_threads`: in this incident, the former omitted the project while the latter retained its task associations and sidebar reference.
5. Repeat the read after a short period: in this incident the project became available again without an agent-initiated repair.

Only one incident has been investigated. Frequency and precise triggering conditions are unknown.

### What is the expected behavior?

Saved local projects should remain visible and accessible after reopening the app. If project loading is still in progress or fails temporarily, show that status and provide a retry instead of making an intact project appear to have disappeared.

The available-project list and task/sidebar project references should converge reliably without requiring users to investigate local state.

### Additional information

The project was pinned and a local registration snapshot was saved only after it had already reappeared. These were visibility/recovery safeguards, not a demonstrated fix.

Private project names, absolute user paths, project/task IDs, conversation content, and raw logs are omitted from this public report.

Potentially related reports: #33727 and #43025. Those describe broader or persistent sidebar/organization problems; this report records a transient omission with persisted registration and task references intact. A shared cause has not been established.

items.title: macOS: Computer Use Screen Recording permission is attached to ChatGPT, not to the helper (com.openai.sky.CUAService) — tool always reports "permissions are still pending"

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: custom-model
labels.description: Issues related to custom model providers (including local models)

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From "About Codex" dialog)?

26.908.70816 (build 9275). Computer Use helper (com.openai.sky.CUAService): 26.913.1001067.

### What subscription do you have?

None — API key mode with a custom model provider (beeapi.ai); the app is not signed in to ChatGPT.

### What platform is your computer?

Darwin 25.6.0 arm64 arm
(macOS 26.6.2, build 25G83, Apple Silicon)

### What issue are you seeing?

Computer Use never becomes usable, even after Screen Recording is granted. Every attempt on any app
returns a permission error forever:

```
com.microsoft.VSCode: Error: Computer Use permissions are still pending. The user has not finished
granting Accessibility and Screen Recording permissions in the ChatGPT Computer Use window. Call this
tool again, as the user is almost done finishing granting permissions. Do not end your turn yet, just
call this tool again.

com.apple.TextEdit: Error: Computer Use permissions are not granted
```

No macOS prompt is ever shown for the helper, and retrying never succeeds.

Root cause (verified from the `tccd` log): the Screen Recording grant lands on the ChatGPT app
(`com.openai.codex`), while the process that actually captures the screen is the separate helper
`com.openai.sky.CUAService` (display name "ChatGPT Computer Use"). Accessibility and Input Monitoring
were granted to the helper correctly, but Screen Recording for the helper is still "not determined",
so its preflight keeps failing.

The UX problem: the guidance says to grant "Accessibility and Screen Recording", the in-app flow and
any macOS prompt lead to the ChatGPT row, and nothing tells the user that "ChatGPT" and
"ChatGPT Computer Use" are two different TCC clients. The helper is also not listed in
System Settings → Screen & System Audio Recording until it asks, so there is nothing to toggle.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Fresh macOS install of the app; grant Screen Recording to "ChatGPT" in
   System Settings → Privacy & Security → Screen & System Audio Recording (as the in-app prompt guides).
2. Grant Accessibility and Input Monitoring to "ChatGPT Computer Use".
3. Fully quit (Cmd+Q) and relaunch the app.
4. In a thread, let Codex use Computer Use on any app, e.g. run the `cua_repl` `js` tool with:
   `let vscode = await cua.getApp('com.microsoft.VSCode');`
5. Observe the error above, permanently, with no prompt.

### What is the expected behavior?

Either

(a) the Screen Recording requirement is requested/attributed to the same client that performs the
capture (`com.openai.sky.CUAService`), so one grant is enough; or
(b) the guidance names the exact System Settings row ("ChatGPT Computer Use") and offers a button that
adds that app to the Screen Recording list, instead of leaving the user to grant the wrong entry.

### Additional information

Evidence from `log show --predicate 'process == "tccd"'` over the 16-minute window in which the helper
repeatedly checked its permissions (authValue: 0 = denied, 1 = not determined, 2 = allowed):

| TCC service              | client                    | verdict                  | count |
|--------------------------|---------------------------|--------------------------|-------|
| kTCCServiceScreenCapture | com.openai.sky.CUAService | 1 (not determined)       | 23    |
| kTCCServiceAccessibility | com.openai.sky.CUAService | 2 (allowed)              | 14    |
| kTCCServiceListenEvent   | com.openai.sky.CUAService | 2 (allowed)              | 9     |
| kTCCServiceScreenCapture | com.openai.codex          | 2 (allowed) / 0 (denied) | 3 / 2 |

Signatures are fine (ruled out): `ChatGPT.app`, `Codex Computer Use.app` and `SkyComputerUseClient.app`
all pass `codesign --verify --deep --strict` and are notarized Developer ID (OpenAI OpCo, LLC,
2DC432GLL2).

Workaround that unblocks Computer Use:
System Settings → Privacy & Security → Screen & System Audio Recording → "+" → `Cmd+Shift+G` →
`/Users/<user>/.codex/computer-use/` → select "Codex Computer Use.app" → enable → fully quit and
relaunch ChatGPT.

The official docs already tell users to check Screen Recording for "Codex Computer Use"
(https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/computer-use), but the app itself never says that this is a different
row from "ChatGPT".

Related issues (searched first, none is the same bug):
#46607 (helper repeatedly asks for first-open approval after updates — Gatekeeper, not TCC),
#22927 ("runtime app is missing"), #18896 (MCP elicitation approval denied per app),
#40394 (Chrome control stopped working), #20556 (screenshot freeze after enabling CUA permissions),
#46276 (app approval dialog never appears).

items.title: [Windows][WSL] Send button stays disabled after the first message (no turn/start is sent)

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

items.body:
### What happens

On Windows with **WSL2 mode enabled** (`[desktop] runCodexInWindowsSubsystemForLinux = true`), a thread only accepts the first message. After that turn finishes, the send button stays greyed out and clicking it does nothing.

- The first message sends and completes normally.
- Then the send button is disabled. Typing still works, but nothing can be submitted.
- The unsent text stays in the composer as a draft (persisted in `composer-prompt-drafts-v2` in the app state).
- Restarting the app does **not** help. Re-opening the thread (which triggers a successful `thread/resume`) does not help either.
- **Workaround that does work:** switch to another thread and back, or start a new thread.

### Environment

- Codex desktop app (Windows, Microsoft Store): **26.915.31945**
- app-server: **0.155.0-alpha.9.2**
- Windows 11 + WSL2 (Ubuntu 24.04)
- Agent mode: full access

### Key observation

After the first turn completes, **no `turn/start` request is ever sent to the app-server** — the message never leaves the UI. So this is a client-side disabled button, not a failed request.

The app log shows turn events being dropped by the renderer, because the conversation lookup uses a turn id where a thread id is expected:

```
error [electron-message-handler] Received turn/started for unknown conversation conversationId=01a0bdb0-cfc6-...
error [electron-message-handler] Received turn/started for unknown conversation conversationId=01a0bdb0-d152-...
error [electron-message-handler] Received turn/completed for unknown conversation conversationId=01a0bdb0-d152-...
```

Because those events are dropped, the per-thread "busy" flag is never cleared. The busy check in the WebView bundle (`app.asar`, decompiled) is:

```js
if (unconfirmedTurnSubmissions?.some(e => e.terminal !== true)) return true;
if (resumeState === 'needs_resume') return threadRuntimeStatus?.type === 'active';
if (turns.length === 0) return resumeState === 'resuming';
return lastTurn(turns)?.status === 'inProgress';
```

Any of these being true disables the composer. The resume response already reports the turn as `completed`, so the state is stuck on one of the other branches.

### Timeline (UTC)

| Time | Event |
|---|---|
| 07:21:17 | 1st message: `turn/start` sent, turn runs |
| 07:23:32 | 1st turn completes (`task_complete`) |
| 07:24 – 07:42 | **18 minutes with zero `turn/start` requests**, while the user was typing and clicking send |
| 07:33:17 | `thread/resume` succeeds (`assignedStreamRole=owner`), button still disabled |
| 07:40 | user switches to another thread and back |
| 07:42:50 | 2nd message finally sends (`turn/start`, took 2.3 s) |

### Possibly related

WSL-mode latency is much worse than Windows-native here: `turn/start` takes ~2.3 s, one `thread/resume` took 17 s, and the app-server request queue overflowed with `App server request expired while queued` (-32001). A single turn also logs hundreds of `[spawn-async] Spawning process inside WSL` lines, which may be related to #46703 (concurrent `wsl.exe` probes crashing the Interop server).

### Regression

Sessions from 2026-09-17 (app **26.911**) contain many messages in one thread. Since 2026-09-19 (app **26.915**), every thread gets exactly one message and then the send button is disabled.
